questions.question: Explain why every General Journal entry requires a narration when the specialised journals never did.
questions.expected_answer: In the column journals the design explains each amount — every CRJ line is money received, every DJ line a credit sale. The GJ records exceptions where no column does the thinking, so each entry must state its own reason ('bad debt written off', 'stock taken by owner'). An unexplained unusual entry would be untraceable and untrustworthy — the narration completes the record.

questions.question: The owner takes stock home for personal use. Explain the entry, and why the amount is at cost rather than selling price.
questions.expected_answer: Debit Drawings, credit Trading Stock (and the debtor is nobody — no sale occurred). The shelf lost goods the business had bought at cost, and the owner withdrew equity in kind; since nothing was sold, no profit margin exists to record — pricing it at selling price would invent income that never happened.

questions.question: Describe the discipline of correcting an error through the GJ: the method, the surgeon's rule, and why erasing is forbidden.
questions.expected_answer: Establish what was done versus what should have been done, then write the entry that moves the books between the two (e.g. debit Stationery, credit Trading Stock R250), with a narration. Correct only the leg that was wrong — redoing the whole transaction double-counts the correct side. Erasing is forbidden because records must be tamper-evident: a visible, dated correction preserves the audit trail that makes the books believable.
